It doesn't have to go through the complicated digestive steps other nutrients do. Inside the mitochondria, it gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate, or α-KG. start: Take 5g a day as a baseline.
old: Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.
new: Take 5g a day as a baseline, to keep your enterocytes fed. Take it away from meals, so it doesn't have to compete with the amino acids in your food to get absorbed. If you train hard or long, like CrossFit or intense cardio, your gut lining takes damage. While you train, your body sends blood away from your gut to your working muscles, so your enterocytes get less oxygen and fuel. Glutamine taken two hours before training helps with that. In a study of men running for an hour in the heat, their gut lining leaked less, even at the lowest dose tested, about 15g for a 70kg man. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure to toxins or pathogens, or your whole system is under a lot of stress, raise it to 10-30g a day, adding 1g a day in case you're sensitive to it. Up to 14g a day is known to be safe for the long run, but the studies of higher doses were too short to say, so come back down once it's over. If you have an active inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), like Crohn's or colitis, don't count on it. In the two small trials in active Crohn's, it didn't help.

old: CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active colon or liver cancer, don't raise the dose that high. new: CAUTION: a lot of cancers feed on glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active cancer, check with your oncologist before you take the 5g, and especially before you go up to the 10-30g. Your enterocytes take in a lot of the glutamine you swallow as soon as it reaches them, but not all of it, and the rest gets into your blood, where a cancer can get to it. They can only take in so much at a time, so the bigger the dose, the more of it gets into your blood.
